title: Slime Rancher
text: God, where to start? I am sure there are tons of other people out there who have glorified this game better than I can, so rather than go crazy about how much I like this game I will just focus on a few highlights. 1 - It isn't that often that you can find a game on Steam that is 100% family friendly.  Sure, there are some games like Subnautica that don't necessarily have swear words or graphic material, but I've had my siblings give it a go and most of them freak out whenever they go outside of the starting zone because of the vast, alien ocean the game takes place in.  This is a game that I could give to my baby niece when she grows old enough to play games and feel confident that I won't be everyone's least favorite uncle.  Would love to see more games like that. 2 - It's music is amazing.  There's nothing to hate about this game's soundtrack.  Every track fits its zone perfectly, be it the rustic farmer track on the Ranch to the upbeat tunes of the Moss Blanket to the mysterious awe of the Glass Desert.  It functions really well with the game's aesthetic which I will get to in a moment. 3 - The game's visuals are like eye candy.  You can never go wrong with making your game focus on toon graphics.  It's pleasing to the eye and brings about less strain on your computer, so you can focus more on adding cool content instead of balancing between something that looks realistic and something that can function on a computer without dropping performance. 4 - It sucks you in.  Literally the first night I played it I spent around 10 hours playing, which would make me feel guilty if not for the fact that I was having a lot of fun.  There are some aspects that do feel grindy, granted - once you establish a working system that sets up the maximum amount of plorts per largo gathering your plorts to get loot can become a chore.  Implementing other means to use said plorts rather than just use it to get currency to spend on cosmetics on your ranch, such as the Slime Scientist Lab, helps break the monotony and gives you an excuse to visit old areas to get new resources.  Even though I finished the base game already I am definitely coming back for more. 5 - It is nice and short.  I beat this game up to 63% achievements in 20 hours, and over half of that was kerfuffing around dealing with stuff in my slime ranch.  Realistically you can beat this game's story in about half that time if you wanted, though I don't recommend you do.  Where this game works well is how everything is balanced together.  There's just the right amount of everything in the experience that you can't just speedrun it.  Take your time and enjoy it, and when you have you'll be able to enjoy one of the sweetest heartfelt endings a simple indie game like this can give.  (Although if you REALLY feel like giving a speedrun a go, there is an optional mode that essentially acts as a 5 hour challenge to get as many newbucks as possible in the allotted timeframe, definitely trying that next). This is a game I'm definitely going to be replaying for a while until I've completed everything, and then I'll definitely give it a replay in the future.  9/10. Before I close this off, if the devs are paying attention, there are a few things I would like to include at the end of this review. - Keep adding content to this game.  It is great, but now I want even more.  I'd love to encounter a volcanic-themed island or perhaps a snow-themed island in the Far Range with equivalent slimes and other resources.  Don't add too much - too much of a good thing won't help anybody - but I would love to see more challenge and more fun like what we got with the Glass Desert.

title: Slime Rancher
text: It is a truly delightful game. 96% positive rating as of this review, and it's easy to see why, after playing it myself. The big thing with this game is that the progression is really rewarding. You go out, grab some slimes, put them in a pen, and feed them to make them poop. Setting aside the beautiful graphics, cuteness overload of the slimes, and the beautiful land to explore, there's just a really good sense of progression. After making some money, by selling the slime poop, you can unlock more plots. You can turn them into additional pens, gardens, chicken coops, storage, etc. Each of these options also has a bunch of useful upgrade available to purchase. After spending a few hours, I really felt like I was making great progress, and I enjoyed every minute of it. There's also a sort of breeding mechanic to the game, where you feed poop from one kind of slime to another kind of slime, and you'll get a hybrid slime. That new slime will eat whatever kind of food the first two liked, and poop two poops each time, Additionally, those poops will be the types you'd get from the original two slimes. It all seems rather like I'm writing notes about the game, but it's really hard to encompass how enjoyable the entire experience is, running around and taking care of things. My advice is, you'd be hard pressed to find a game that's quite like this.

title: Slime Rancher
text: A blatantly overrated game. Though enjoyable, it fails to provide motives to play further. I advise buying when on sale with at the very least a 50% cut-off. + Cute graphics and cute slime creatures + Very original gameplay + It's exciting to explore the world (at least at first) + Simple farming mechanics + Jetpack flight! - All slimes are basically the same - There is nothing to do in the different locations - Lack sidequests and secondary objectives - Daily objectives are poorly rewarded, making them irrelevant - There is a lot of treasures on the map that you can only open in the late game - Poorly designed teleportation system - Very bad aiming - No story of any sort - No background for the main character (exept poorly written mail that you receive occasionally) - No lore Slime Rancher is nice at first sight, and its mix of farming and FPS is both intriguing and enjoyable. Alas, there is no incentive to play and the game is mostly purposeless. Exploration is not that rewarding and new locations are just the same as before, with new colors. It would have been better with secrets, side quests, and small objectives. Slime Rancher is a farming game mixed with an FPS. You own a ranch, where you raise slimes, harmless bubble-like creatures, which produces a magical brighly-colored poo called 'plort' which, for some reason, is worth a good deal of money. You can also grow vegetables and chickens to feed the slimes according to their preferences. That's about all for the farming part, though you must take care to provide good living conditions for the different slimes (e.g. fireflies slimes cannot stand daylight so you must protect them). The interest of the game lies in the exploration part. To capture new kind of slimes, you must go into the wild armed with some kind of a vacuum cleaner which can absorb slimes and all sorts of objects (chickens, vegetables, plorts). As the capacity of your vacuum cleaner is drastically reduced (you can only carry four different kinds of items, all in limited quantities), it means a lot of backtracking since you constantly have to go back to your ranch to bring back your loot. To unlock new locations, you must find a key which is given by the bursting of a giant slime thanks to your overfeeding it. It's a bit cruel, but fine. New locations mean new kind of graphical textures, and new slimes. A teleporter can bring you back to the ranch, but it's one-way only for most of them (actually the teleportation system is extremely confusing). When you die, you loose everything you carry and you get to sleep for hours (in the meanwhile slimes can escape their corral and wreak havoc in your farm by eating all the chickens). As the jumping system is not that great, it means that you can waste all your loot just for falling into the water. It seems a bit cheap. The money you get by selling plorts can be used to improve your ranch (e.g. unlocking new parts of it) and the living conditions of your slimes, or to upgrade your staff (jetpack, carrying capacity, health). Additionnally, you have daily objectives. They are trade offers from other slime ranchers (that you will never get to meet in real). Usually it's not that interesting and not worth the trouble. Also, you find treasure spheres during your explorations. Unfortunately, you cannot open them unless you are in the late game. Which means, until then, exploring carefully all the caves and places is basically pointless. It's a bit disappointing that exploration is not rewarded to begin with. And that's about it. I think this little description fairly covers all the main aspects of the game. In my opinion, it's not enough to provide a good reason to play. I enjoyed the few hours I spent with the game but I cannot be certain I will keep playing it in the future. Due to an overall lack of small objectives, there is no "one more thing to do and I quit" effect and you can lose interest pretty fast. Without story, without purpose except making good money, without special fun in the FPS part (I mean, you just collect the slimes, there is no fight of any kind), the game certainly feels a bit bland.

title: Snake Pass
text: For the price point, I think Sumo totally knocked this game out of the park. What you get is 15 smallish to decent sized collectathon levels with gorgeous design and lots of strange platforming to figure out. Personally, I loved it! I prefered discovering the strange controls of this game to jumping around in most other platformers. I feel like Snake Pass takes a genre that kind of falls into tropes, embraces those tropes (graphic style, collectables, nifty companion) but then takes the one trope that defines the genre (aka controls) and totally flips that on it's head. So how do the controls feel? They feel great! After a few minutes of practice, they allow you to wrap around poles and slither through grass like I imagine a snake would be able to. They are strange, but towards the end of the game they felt totally natural to me. It's a good thing they are good as well because it's kind of the main draw here. I liked this game and if you want a 3D platformer, I think you will like it to and appreciate the way it twists the genre.

title: Snake Pass
text: Before I bought this game, I didn't know what genre to expect, since you're a snake and you slide/slither across instead of jumping like you do in most, if not all, platformers. So I was sort of dumbfounded about it, but now I know! Clearly, it's a 3D platformer. Why? The horrendous, atrocious camera and controls that have plagued most 3D platformers since the early 32-bit console days are present here, in full glory. And in my case, they're without a doubt, the absolute worst I've come across since the PSX era. The camera intentionally obscures what's around you and instead focuses on the ground most of the time. This is to try and make the game "challenging" somehow, otherwise they simply would have included a locked camera mode, as an option at least, with an isometric angle when it gets too close to the character or an object. The controls too get in the way, 'grip' for instance doesn't do what it's supposed to and it's a struggle and a chore just to get over a small obstacle or climbing a short pole or stick, this is exacerbated by clipping issues and off course, the drunk, inept, camera sabotaging every move and action. A big disappointment, a pity really. The game is indeed charming, and the music is great and it makes you happy, at least when you're in the main menu, cause instead of being a relaxing and a chill game like you thought it would be, it ends up being extremely infuriating and exasperating. You always end up fighting the camera and controls, nothing enjoyable in the slightest.

title: Snake Pass
text: I'm only two hours in, but I'm writing a recommendation anyway. This is ingenious. No matter how experienced you think you are with games, this is going to test you. It looks like a typical platformer with a lot of objects to collect, but unlike other platformers these aren't simply tokens, coins and gems. Think of them as goals, and there's a physics puzzle in the way for you to solve: how will I reach that? There are only three objects that you must collect in each level to move on, so there's a lot of replay value in going back later and figuring out how to get the stuff you missed. The best part is the control system for the snake. Maybe you've seen videos and assumed that the movement must be scripted, but it isn't. You have to thread the snake's body around the scaffolding of poles, tighten its coils around branches, and guide the creature's head to wind onto the next stick. Every movement is deliberate. It's at once relaxing and tense, and the translation of analogue stick controls and trigger pulls to the snake's movement is surprisingly natural. It's a complex and challenging gameplay system, and it's constantly joyful. I don't think we get enough true brilliance and beauty in games, so this is to be celebrated.

text: This is the most frustrating game that I have ever enjoyed. The optional stuff is surprisingly hard, and the physics-based platforming is very tricky to do well. It's not just a case of timing your jumps. You have to worm your way around obstacles, grip/release them, build up momentum, aim your head in 3D-space, and do all sorts of complicated movements. It's just really hard to get used to it, and it will have you screaming at the TV when things go wrong. Stuff that is really easy in other platformers is incredibly hard when you're a snake. Overall great game though. The camera annoyed me a bit at times, with background scenery getting in the way, but that's pretty much the only major complaint. The music's great too.

title: Snakebird
text: Well, see what comes out of fervently wishing for something. I've loved the indie puzzle revolution of recent years, I only wished for more difficult, more challenging puzzles, because it was really celebration time if a game produced at least a few levels that made your neurons sweat a little. And now enter Snakebird, a cute, nice-looking little game, which is really a ruthless killer of a puzzle game in candy-flavoured disguise. Snakebird wants you to collect all the fruits on a level and proceding to the exit with every one of your characters. Eating a fruit grows your snakebird with one unit, gravity works in the game, some levels provide you with simple items to help your progress, while the environment sometimes wants to kill you. There. That's it, really - and a collection of really, really tough levels, which manage to be hard without being unfair. Snakebird is easily the best (non-construction) puzzle game I've played in a long while - I bow before the greatness of the people who designed its levels. For those who are looking for a serious brainy challenge - highly recommended.

title: Snakebird
text: So Snakebird starts out decently enough but quickly devolves down into an obnoxious brute force "puzzle" game. Here's the game in a nutshell. Levels are laid out as a square grid. You'll control 1-3 snakes which will each be a certain number of squares long. On levels with multiple snakes, pressing tab will select a different one. Some levels will have fruit. If it has fruit, you must eat the fruit with a snake which will make the snake 1 square bigger. Once all fruit is eaten, the exit to the level opens. If there's no fruit, then the exit begins open and you must navigate your snake(s) to the exit. The trick to the game is that the snakes will fall based on their current shape if they're no longer touching the ground. So you often need to shape your snake a particular way so falling causes it to land on a platform rather than a spike trap or off the bottom of the level. Snakes can also push each other if you ram another one, you'll often need to do this to get another snake to certain spots. At any time, you can reset a level or press backspace to undo moves as far as you want. If you die, the game automatically undoes your last move. The music and graphics are fine. The game controls decently well. It starts out fine enough but quickly shows its ugly head. Minor Quibble: If you're moving your snake around to solve the 'puzzles' and die on a level (and you will die many times) the game backs up 1 turn. If you have multiple snakes, the game selects the snake that died rather than the snake that moved. So once the game undoes your move, you'll go to move the snake you were using only to discover that the game has selected the other snake as the active snake instead. So you've driven that snake somewhere you didn't want it to go and have to undo moves and then select the other snake. This is a minor issue, but it will happen very frequently and is annoying. Why not just leave the active snake as the active snake when the death gets undone? I can't imagine what sort of idiotic reasoning the game designers had for making it this way. So the biggest problem this game has is that each level isn't so much a puzzle as it is a brute force method of elimination. Most levels require that your snake(s) be moved in a specific manner. If you do not move in the exact manner the level designer wants you to, you will fail.  Quick example:  You need to move somewhere 4 spaces away, so you could choose to move (up, up, right, right) or (right, right, up up) or (up, right, up, right) or (right, up, right, up).  All viable right?  Well not in Snakebird.  In Snakebird, only one of those choices might allow you to succeed.  Now imagine your Snake is bigger and/or you have multiple snakes, all of which must move in specific manners.  This is what you do every single level.  All you're really doing is making a best guess as to whether a path you're taking is the right one until you either succeed or eliminate every possibility it contains and then do the same for some other path until you finally pick the right pathway. There's never really any moments where you get excited or feel good for figuring something out, you just go “Well, I guessed the correct path that 23rd time”. It feels as though the level designers made the levels starting at the end rather then the beginning, traced a specific path that each snake must make from the end back to a certain point, then set that as the start point, and then designed the levels around the pre-made paths. Levels are designed in a way that you could divide them up into several parts. You might clear 1 or 2 parts only to discover at part 3 that you didn't clear part 1 or 2 in the specific manner you were supposed to.  Have fun going back to part 2 or maybe all the way back to part 1. After brute forcing my way through several levels, I'd had enough. I never felt like I was doing something thoughtful but instead was just punishing myself looking for that 1 and only 1 specific path. It feels like a mindless grind rather than something thought provoking that lead to a solution. Edit: To further clarify since I've had some comments. I never claimed there's anything wrong with one pathway puzzle games, I enjoy plenty of them. The problem is that this one is a lemon. It offers nothing thoughtful.  Snakebird is a maze variant.  The best strategy for beating a maze?  Start at the end and work backwards, it's the same here in Snakebird.  This is a strategy I figured out for mazes by the age of 5-6.  If you consider tracing paths backwards to be thought provoking and a real brain burner, boy are you in for a treat. Consider this: All you do in the game is move up, left, right, & down and on some levels switch your snakes. Sounds incredibly simple right? We should all be able to beat a game this simple in a few hours right? So, how do you extend the playtime of something this simple? Easy, make it unfair. People seem confused about the brute forcing parts, so I'm going to ELI 8 this for people. Let's look at how you play a maze, there are 2 methods.  1. Draw as you go:  You use a pencil, start at the start point and draw a path until you reach an area where you can go in multiple directions (a decision point).  You then glance at the maze and make a best guess which way to go.  If it leads to another decision point, do the same thing.  If it leads to a dead end, you erase your path back to the decision point, glance at the maze, and make a new best guess.  Repeat until you get to the exit.  2. Trace and then draw:  This works the same exact way as number 1, except you wait to draw your path until you've traced your way to the exit.  It's important to note that it doesn't matter whether you actually drew a path into a dead end or traced your finger into a dead end, you ran into the dead end.  They are the same exact things.  Mazes don't require intelligence to solve.  The best you can do at any given point is make a best guess where you should go and do that over and over and over until it succeeds.  This is brute forcing.  Now let's look at Snakebird.  How can you play Snakebird?  Well, there are 2 ways.  Let's assume we're on a level with 3 fruits.  1. Move as you play:  In this method, you move your Snakebird until you hit a decision point.  You glance at all the fruit and make a best guess as to which one you can get.  You then move your Snakebird to it and attempt to get it.  If you get it, you glance at the remaining fruit and make a new best guess as to which one you can get.  If you fail to get the fruit (either because you're too short, you block yourself out, you fall into the abyss, or fall into a spike), then you undo your moves until you're back at the decision point, glance at the remaining fruit, and make a new best guess.  Repeat until you get all fruit and into the exit.  2: Trace and then move:  This works the same exact way as number 1, except you wait to move your Snakebird until you've successfully traced a working path to a piece of fruit or to all fruits and into the exit.  Again, it's important to note that it doesn't matter whether you moved your Snakebird and fell off a ledge/onto a spike or traced a path where you realized your Snakebird would fall off a ledge/onto a spike, you still died.  They are the exact same things.  The problems with Snakebird are the exact same problems a maze has.  You're simply brute forcing best guesses until they work.  Again, it doesn't matter whether you're actually moving your Snakebird around or just tracing paths in your head, you're doing the exact same things. If you want to see exactly what I'm talking about, one of the commenters has videos of himself playing this.  Click on the comments, find the profile of “Edderiofer” (who does not agree with the way I reviewed this game) and click on his profile.  Then take 2-5 minutes to watch a video of him playing this game to see solid evidence that what I've written is entirely accurate.

text: I hate this game. I ragequit and launched it again 10 times in an hour. That's the mindset it may put you into. It is a really clever puzzle game. Unlike the all-too-common unfair games of this genre that go for the "reverse-engineering" of the random problem the creator put up by toying around, the puzzles in this one are real thinkers : you understand pretty quickly what you are supposed to do (though not always, I'll get back to that), but you'll be torturing yourself trying to actually get there. Solving puzzles in this condition feels very rewarding. Sadly there is a drawback associated with this : the game doesn't tell you anything. You have to figure everything out yourself, and when the game throws new elements you weren't expecting to be interactive, it will just get you confused as to what to do. I think a simple explanations of a few basic mechanics early in the game wouldn't have spoiled the experience, quite the contrary. The game saves the current puzzle in the state you left it on quit - but leave a level to the map and all your progress is lost. personally I'd wish it saved an instance of every puzzles so you could mix and go between them as you wish, without pressure. And yeah, the thing is ♥♥♥♥ing cute. 30 puzzles to go at the time of this review!

title: Snakebird

Snakebird adds to the sliding tile puzzle by adding the effect of gravity. So now, the complications have doubled. You have to plan for how the Snakebird can fall. I fear that this is too tough for me.

text: First of all - i've played this game mostly in offline mode due some issues with my ISP, so gameplay time doesn't reflect reality (actually i've spent over 10 hrs in game). Game was overall huge disappointment for me and it doesn't matter game perfectly reflects one of crucial WW aspects (trying to stop Nazis from building V2 and even more powerful a-bomb). I was teased with stealth game which is simply not stealth. Yes, game has stealth mechanics like checking if enemy sees you or hears you, you can hide and silently crawl, you can distract enemies ... but there any stealth ends. Literally in each mission it is only matter of time when you get into situation when everyone on actual map is aware of your position, no matter where are you hiding. Each mission, no matter how carefuly and stealthy you are, turns into third person shooter. So i am disappointed as game was presented like stealth, but unfortunately it is just another common WW generic shooter with really narrow corridors/maps. One of only few games i had no taste to finish it, unfortunately. I do not reccomend it to anyone who is interested in being stealthy sniper. Go for Sniper Ghost Warrior. + based on true events during WW + not bad graphics + nice audio design + controls + game takes in count things like balistic or where exactly did you shoot your enemy + nice demonstration what sniper rifle can do in bullet times (one can learn from anatomy ;) a lot) - not so stealth game, even it posseses stealth mechanics - no knife/hand kill i.e. from behind - levels are really tight and narrow corridors masked for streets of Berlin
